 Millions of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) recipients in 46 states could face the loss of their benefits if a new rule proposed by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) takes effect. The department, which oversees the largest food-nutrition program in the country, is seeking to limit how states use Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program services to help people qualify for SNAP. If enacted, the rule could cause as many as 6.3 million people to lose benefits, according to the USDA. If enacted and fully implemented, the rule could push as many as 6.3 million people off the program by fiscal year 2029, the USDA said. Newsweek has contacted the USDA for comment via email. The Trump administration has overseen considerable changes to the SNAP program since January 2025, including expanded work requirements and restrictions on what recipients can buy in some states. SNAP participation has already fallen sharply, largely due to federal policy changes enacted in 2025. Just over 36 million people received food stamps in July 2026, the latest month for which data is available, compared with approximately 41.6 million a year earlier. The decline comes amid changes to SNAP eligibility, including expanded work requirements, although the extent to which individual policies have contributed to the fall is unclear. Proposed Changes The USDA has proposed narrowing the rules that let states use Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE) to qualify households for SNAP. According to the USDA, 46 state agencies had adopted BBCE as of December 2025, allowing households receiving certain non-cash TANF benefits to qualify for SNAP. Depending on state policy, BBCE can let some households qualify for SNAP even if their income is above the usual federal gross income limit. It can also mean the state does not apply the SNAP asset test to those households. The proposed rule would stop states from allowing TANF-funded services that are not classed as "assistance" to confer categorical eligibility. Households would instead need to receive TANF assistance—mostly cash, but also certain supports to help meet ongoing basic needs, such as childcare and transportation assistance for unemployed parents—to qualify categorically through TANF. In its rule, the USDA cites instances of "benefits of nominal value, such as an informational pamphlet or an 800-number to call to locate TANF-funded services," being used to grant eligibility. It would not automatically end SNAP benefits for everyone who qualifies through BBCE, but would change how states determine eligibility and require state SNAP agencies to assess more households under standard SNAP income and asset eligibility rules. The USDA estimates the rule, if enacted, could push some 6.3 million people across 3.2 million households off the program in fiscal year 2029, when the department expects the rule to have its full effect. The changes would make SNAP eligibility more standardized and "preserve benefits for the truly needy," the ‌rule ⁠reads. The change would reduce benefits by $44.649 billion over the five-year period between 2027 and 2031, the USDA estimates. The proposal could also affect access to other nutrition programs. The USDA estimates that approximately 1.78 million children would lose automatic eligibility for free school meals, although around 97 percent would remain eligible for free or reduced-price meals through a separate application process. Opposition The proposed rule has drawn condemnation from Democrats and advocacy groups. Representative Angie Craig of Minnesota said the rule was "heartless and cruel." "The proposed rule would make it harder to meet basic needs and roll back efforts to streamline federal programs," she said in a November 9 statement. "SNAP is a highly effective and efficient program when it is allowed to work as designed. Unfortunately, the Trump administration and the outgoing Republican majority in Congress have undermined the program’s integrity at every turn, harming millions of vulnerable Americans in the process." George Kelemen, senior vice president of Share Our Strength, said the proposed rule "is yet another blow to the families working hard to put food on the table." He said: "Already, 5.5 million Americans have lost SNAP since Congress passed historic cuts last summer, including an estimated 2 million children nationwide," he said. "This proposal, along with the other harmful policies to weaken nutrition programs, will worsen our growing hunger crisis." What Happens Next The rule is currently open for public comment in the Federal Register until December 10. The USDA will consider public comments before deciding whether to finalize the proposal.
